query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, the maintenance of a self‐organized, fine-scale lamellar microstructure—comprising an alternating soft FCC matrix and a hard, ordered B2 phase (enriched in Al/Ni)—is the critical mechanistic factor governing phase stability. This lamellar architecture, achieved via tailored thermo‐mechanical processing, stabilizes the phase distribution against coarsening and environment‐induced degradation, thereby retaining high‐temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or conventionally processed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with relatively coarse or inhomogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply designed thermo‐mechanical processing (e.g., controlled cooling, rolling, and annealing) to produce a fine, self-organized lamellar microstructure with alternating FCC and B2 phases.
generation.conditions: Controlled laboratory experiments at varying temperatures, including high-temperature exposure, corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing acid), and cryogenic testing, with identical nominal alloy compositions for processed (lamellar) and unprocessed (baseline) samples.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined lamellar architecture consisting of a soft FCC phase and a hard, ordered B2 phase.
generation.mechanism: The lamellar structure restricts diffusion and impedes phase coarsening under thermal and environmental stresses. The B2 phase, enriched in Al/Ni, promotes oxidation resistance and acts as a barrier to radiation damage, while the ductile FCC matrix supports toughness, particularly at cryogenic temperatures. Together, they yield a synergistic effect that preserves the desirable mechanical and environmental properties over a wide range of conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the processed alloy will exhibit (i) minimal phase coarsening and stable phase fractions after prolonged high-temperature exposure, (ii) superior resistance to corrosion and oxidation as evidenced by more stable passive film compositions, (iii) higher retained yield and fracture toughness under radiation exposure, and (iv) improved ductility at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs produced without targeted thermo‐mechanical processing that lack a well-defined lamellar microstructure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable primarily to alloys with near-equiatomic compositions in the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system processed via routes amenable to controlled lamellar formation. Deviations in composition or processing that significantly alter the phase partitioning or produce completely different microstructures may fall outside the hypothesis’ domain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative effects on each property (e.g., extent of mechanical property retention or specific resistance levels to environmental degradation) are uncertain and may depend on the details of the processing parameters and testing environments. Furthermore, the interplay of radiation effects with the microstructural stability of the lamellar architecture requires further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples with identical compositions: one set will undergo a tailored thermo‐mechanical processing route to generate a fine lamellar (FCC + B2) microstructure, and the other will remain in an as-cast state with a coarser or less uniform microstructure. Subject both sets to prolonged high-temperature exposure, corrosive environmental testing (e.g., chloride-containing acid at various temperatures), radiation exposure (or simulated radiation damage), and cryogenic mechanical testing.
measurements: Phase distribution and stability via X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy before and after environmental exposure
Mechanical properties (yield strength, fracture toughness, ductility) at high temperature and cryogenic temperatures
Corrosion and oxidation resistance characterized by electrochemical tests and surface spectroscopy
Radiation damage tolerance tested through ion irradiation and subsequent microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed lamellar samples do not show statistically significant improvements in phase stability (i.e., minimal coarsening or phase evolution) and in the targeted mechanical and environmental properties relative to the as-cast baseline under the test conditions, then the proposed hypothesis—that the lamellar microstructure is the critical factor governing phase stability and the associated property retention—would be falsified.

A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperatures

Abstract: In this work, the influence of temperature on the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution was investigated using electrochemical measurement, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Results show that the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, while an unstable film forms on the alloy at high temperatures. Furthermore, temperature changes the proportion of hydroxide and oxide in Fe and Cr, but it has no noticeable effect on Al and Ni, which is a significant factor on the passive behavior. L12 phase exhibits good corrosion resistance at different temperatures. Pitting occurred on B2 phase in the chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution at a low temperature of 5 °C, while pitting and dissolution take place on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the acid solution at room temperature and above.

Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata

Abstract: AbstractTogether with the thermodynamics and kinetics, the complex microstructure of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exerts a significant influence on the associated oxidation mechanisms in these concentrated solid solutions. To describe the surface oxidation in AlCoCrFeNi HEA, we employed a stochastic cellular automata model that replicates the mesoscale structures that form. The model benefits from diffusion coefficients of the principal elements through the native oxides predicted by using molecular simulations. Through our examination of the oxidation behavior as a function of the alloy composition, we corroborated that the oxide scale growth is a function of the complex chemistry and resultant microstructures. The effect of heat treatment on these alloys is also simulated by using reconstructed experimental micrographs. When they are in a single-crystal structure, no segregation is noted for α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3, which are the primary scale-forming oxides.
